items.title: George "Tex" Stephens Interview, 1995-08-29
items.q: you had anybody coming in like some of the big-time bands like maybe Erskine Hawkins, maybe Bo Moose Jackson or Billie Holiday

ctx.x: Was that, would you say, that that was true of most establishments, black establishments in the city?

No, well, you were a little more relaxed than some of the other clubs. If you went down to Albert Ellis' Horseshoe Lounge, you could be well-dressed, but you could go without a collar or a tie. You just show up and you could be there, and if you would go to Booker T. Washington, maybe you would probably, at that time, you would probably dress a little more because we were proud to have Booker T. Washington Auditorium because it was a new facility, and it was a little better than the Rosenwald thing down the…
Yeah. Yeah. It's a new day. It's a new day. Okay, where were we? Okay, so after, I mean after the Sentinel, where, what other, did you work for another paper after that?

ctx.x: Oh, I'm fine. It'll pick up. It always picks up. Okay, we'll continue with Tech Stevens. This is the, let's make sure this one's working. Okay, continuing with Tech Stevens. Today is August the 23rd. I think it's 23rd, Saturday 23rd. We're at Tulane University. My name's Tad Jones, and we're with Techs. So we were going to pick up, go back and listen to, you know, talk about some other, some things that we left off.

We left off. Yeah, well let's fill in where we left off. Let's go back to the 40s and we'll update things. Some of the things we didn't cover, like when Oyskin Hawkins came here in 1949. He played at the Booker T. Washington Auditorium. And incidentally, Mabel Scott played at Foster's Rainbow Room, and Gate Mouth Brown played together. And then they went over to the Dewdrop, and they did a midnight show like that was back there in 1949. And I think I discussed with you earlier about Amos Milburn and Winoni Harris…
